screens.title: Basic CRUD Operations with mongosh
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build fundamental fluency with the mongosh interactive shell. We begin by switching to or creating a database, then insert single and multiple documents, query with operators, update fields safely using update operators, and finally remove documents with care. These operations are the bread and butter of application data work: inserting records when users submit forms, querying to display results, updating to reflect state changes, and deleting when data is removed. A concrete example you will practice is managing a small products collection — inserting a Laptop Pro, querying by brand or price, incrementing stock, and deleting out-of-stock items. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls, such as accidentally replacing entire documents when you forget to use update operators, or removing everything by passing an empty filter to deleteMany. By the end you’ll understand each CRUD method syntax, when to use single‑document versus multi‑document variants, and how to craft filters with operators like $gt, $lt, and $in. Keep an eye out for the hands-on bookstore activity where you’ll try these commands yourself and confirm each change using find and findOne. Ready to begin and see how these commands map to real application needs?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Basic CRUD Operations
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Basic CRUD Operations with mongosh

Practice the essential shell commands that add, read, change, and remove documents in MongoDB. These actions support every data-driven feature in an application.

In this lesson
Insert documents, query with operators, perform safe updates, and delete with filters.
Why it matters
CRUD operations map directly to user actions: saves, searches, edits, and removals.
Coming up
A hands-on bookstore activity to practice commands end-to-end.
Products collection
A simple inventory used across examples
Create
insertOne / insertMany — add documents and let MongoDB generate _id.
Read
find / findOne with query operators like $gt or $in.
Update
updateOne / updateMany with $set, $inc, $push to modify fields safely.
Explore Key Topics
Insert patterns — single vs many
Query operators — $gt, $lt, $in
Safe updates — use operators

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice on the essential actions in mongosh and why each matters. First, you will perform CRUD operations in mongosh, which means using insertOne and insertMany to add records, find and findOne to query them, updateOne and updateMany to change them, and deleteOne and deleteMany to remove them. Practically, this means you can build features like product listing, search filters, inventory adjustments, and controlled removals. Second, you'll learn to craft query filters with operators such as $gt, $lt, $in and logical operators like $or and $and so you can select exactly the documents you need. Third, you will use update operators such as $set, $inc, and $push to change fields without overwriting entire documents, avoiding a common data-loss mistake. Finally, you'll practice safe deletion patterns and verification steps so you never accidentally remove the wrong records. Each objective pairs a command with a real example and a short verification step so you can measure your competence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide zooms into patterns and verification steps you need to be reliable. You will practice using the use command to select or implicitly create a database, so you understand where your collections live and how MongoDB creates them on first insert. You will learn to inspect operation results: insertOne returns an insertedId and acknowledged status; update operations return matched and modified counts; delete commands return deleted counts. Recognizing these outputs helps verify success without blindly trusting state. You will also practice distinguishing single‑document commands from multi‑document variants and when each is appropriate — for user edits use updateOne, for sweeping changes across many records use updateMany combined with careful filters. Lastly, you will rehearse safety checks such as running a find with the same filter before executing deleteMany. This reduces catastrophic mistakes and builds a habit of verification.

keyIdea.title: Verification focus
keyIdea.text: Read operation outputs and confirm results with find before and after updates or deletions to prevent unintended changes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Learning Objectives — Part 2
Database and operation patterns
  • Use the use <dbname> command to select or implicitly create a database when you insert documents.
  • Check results: insertOne returns insertedId; updateOne shows matched and modified counts; deleteOne returns deletedCount.
  • Choose single vs many: use updateOne/deleteOne for targeted changes; updateMany/deleteMany for batch changes with careful filters.
  • Always run a verification find before destructive operations to confirm the filter matches intended documents.
Common pitfall mnemonic
For updates, remember: forgetting the $ operator replaces the entire document. For deletes, remember: an empty filter removes everything. Make it a habit to preview results.
Preview
Run find(filter).pretty() to confirm targets.
Check result
Read insertedId, matchedCount, modifiedCount, deletedCount.

screens.title: Selecting a Database with use and implicit creation
screens.narratorSegment: Switching to the correct database is the first step in any shell workflow. The mongosh command use myStore doesn't throw an error if the database doesn't yet exist; instead MongoDB will implicitly create the database and any collection inside it when you first insert data. This behavior matters because operations like insertOne and insertMany will determine where your documents are stored based on the current database. A concrete example: running use myStore and then db. products. insertOne({ name: "Laptop Pro", price: 1200 }) creates myStore and a products collection if they didn't exist before. A common misconception is believing use creates a persistent database immediately; it only reserves the name until there is real data inserted. Another pitfall is running commands in the wrong database because you forgot to call use — your insert may quietly go to a different database. To avoid this, adopt a quick verification step: after switching, run show collections or a simple find to confirm the target collection exists or is empty. Takeaway: always set and verify your database context before mutating data to keep operations deterministic and safe.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Select Database
Core Concept

use <dbname> and implicit creation

Switching context determines where insertions and queries operate. Creation occurs on first insert, not when you run use.

Quick terminal example
use myStore
// switch to myStore
// now insert to implicitly create database and collection

db.products.insertOne({
  name: "Laptop Pro",
  brand: "TechCorp",
  price: 1200.00
})

show collections
// products will appear after insert
Explanation
  • use only sets shell context. The database becomes persistent once data is inserted.
  • Inserting into db.collection triggers creation of the database and collection if absent.
  • Always confirm context with show collections or a harmless find before critical writes.
Analogy
Think of use as opening a folder in a file explorer. The folder only exists on disk after you save a file into it.
Key Takeaway

Set and verify your database context before inserting data to avoid writing to the wrong location.

screens.title: Inserting Documents with insertOne and insertMany
screens.narratorSegment: Inserting documents is how you create persistent records in MongoDB. Use insertOne when you need to add a single document and insertMany when adding a batch. Each insert returns a result object: insertOne gives you acknowledged and insertedId; insertMany returns acknowledged and an array of insertedIds. For example, insertOne with a product document will return insertedId which you can then use to query that document. insertMany is useful during bulk imports — here you receive a map of inserted ids so you can cross-reference them or log creation. A common mistake is assuming insertMany is atomic across documents; while it inserts many documents in one call, partial failures can occur depending on options like ordered:false. Another pitfall is relying solely on the shell output without verifying with a find. After inserting, run db. collection. find({ _id: insertedId }) or db. collection. find(). pretty() to confirm. Takeaway: choose insertOne for individual writes, insertMany for batches, and always verify inserted IDs to ensure no silent failures. Inserting Documents with insertOne and insertMany means always read the returned insertedid(s) and perform a verification query to confirm the inserted documents exist as expected.. In practical terms, add single or multiple documents and verify insertion results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always read the returned insertedId(s) and perform a verification query to confirm the inserted documents exist as expected.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Insert Documents
Definition

insertOne and insertMany

Use insertOne for a single document and insertMany for multiple documents. Each method returns the inserted id(s) so you can verify success.

db.products.insertOne({
  name: "Laptop Pro",
  brand: "TechCorp",
  price: 1200.00,
  stock: 50
})

// insertMany

db.products.insertMany([
  { name: "Mechanical Keyboard", brand: "KeyMaster", price: 95.5 },
  { name: "Wireless Mouse", brand: "ClickTech", price: 35.0 }
])
Why it matters
Inserts create the data your application displays. Verifying insertedId prevents confusion during subsequent operations that rely on a newly-created document.
Verification steps
  • Read insertedId from the result object.
  • Run db.products.find({ _id: insertedId }) to confirm.
  • For insertMany, check insertedIds array and run a sample find for one or two ids.
Key Takeaway

Insert operations return identifiers you should check; don’t assume inserts succeeded without verification.

screens.title: Querying with find() and findOne()
screens.narratorSegment: Queries are how you read data out of MongoDB. The primary methods are find, which returns a cursor that can match many documents, and findOne, which returns the first matching document. When you call find without a filter it returns all documents; when you pass a filter document you specify exact field conditions. For example, db. products. find({ brand: "TechCorp" }). pretty() returns all TechCorp items, while db. products. findOne({ name: "Laptop Pro" }) returns a single product. It’s important to understand how query operators extend filters: using price: { $gt: 100 } selects documents where price is greater than 100. A common misconception is expecting find to return an array immediately; instead it returns a cursor you iterate or print. In mongosh, chaining. pretty() formats output for readability. Takeaway: choose find when you expect multiple matches and findOne when a single result suffices, and always use filters and operators to limit data scanned for performance and correctness. Querying with find() and findOne() means use find for multi-document results and findone for a single match; always apply filters and operators to narrow results.. In practical terms, retrieve documents and use filters to narrow results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Querying data
Core Concept

find() vs findOne()

Use find for sets and findOne for a single document. Filters narrow results and improve correctness and performance.

// find all
db.products.find().pretty()

// find by brand
db.products.find({ brand: "TechCorp" }).pretty()

// find documents price > 100 and stock < 100
db.products.find({ price: { $gt: 100 }, stock: { $lt: 100 } }).pretty()

// single match
db.products.findOne({ name: "Laptop Pro" })
Query operators
Operators like $eq, $gt, $lt, $in let you express ranges and sets. $or and $and compose complex conditions for precise matches.
Misconception
find returns a cursor, not a raw array. Use cursor methods or chaining like .pretty() in the shell to view results.
Key Takeaway

Apply filters and operators to target documents; prefer findOne for a single known match and find for lists.

screens.title: Query Operators — Filters and Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Query operators are the tools that let you find exactly the documents you need. Numeric comparison operators like $gt and $lt let you select values above or below thresholds — for example, price: { $gt: 100 } finds items costing more than one hundred. The $in operator matches any value in a provided array, useful for brands or enum fields. Logical operators $or and $and let you combine clauses: $or selects documents matching any clause, while $and requires all clauses to be true. A practical example: to find items from KeyMaster or ClickTech you can use { $or: [ { brand: "KeyMaster" }, { brand: "ClickTech" } ] }. Another example: find products with features containing "RGB Backlight" by querying the array directly with features: "RGB Backlight". A common misunderstanding is thinking $in is a subset test; it matches any listed value, not require all. Also avoid overly broad filters that unintentionally match many documents. Takeaway: use operators to narrow results precisely and test queries with find() before using them in updates or deletes. Query Operators — Filters and Logic means combine comparison and logical operators to build exact filters; test filters before using them in write operations.. In practical terms, how $gt, $lt, $in, $or and $and let you express precise conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Query Operators
Comparison

Common operators

  • $gt / $lt / $gte / $lte — numeric comparisons for ranges.
  • $in / $nin — match any or none of the values in an array.
  • $and / $or — compose clauses for complex logic.
// price greater than 100 and stock less than 100

db.products.find({ price: { $gt: 100 }, stock: { $lt: 100 } }).pretty()

// brand in a set

db.products.find({ brand: { $in: ["KeyMaster", "ClickTech"] } }).pretty()

// logical OR

db.products.find({ $or: [{ brand: "KeyMaster" }, { brand: "ClickTech" }] }).pretty()
Array query
To find documents containing an array element, query the array field directly. For example features: "RGB Backlight" matches items whose features array includes that string.
Misconception
$in does not require all values be present — it matches if any value in the list appears. For all values, you must design a different filter or use $all where applicable.
Key Takeaway

Use operators to narrowly express conditions, and test filters before running updates or deletes.

screens.title: Updating Documents with updateOne and updateMany
screens.narratorSegment: Updating documents in MongoDB requires care: an update without an operator will replace the entire document. That's why updateOne and updateMany take an update document that typically contains update operators such as $set to change specific fields, $inc to increment numeric values, and $push to append to arrays. For example, to set a new price and increment stock for a single product you can run an updateOne with a filter on name and an update document that includes $set: { price: 1250.00 } and $inc: { stock: 5 }. For a brand-wide change, updateMany with the same operators applies to all matching documents. Inspect the result to read matchedCount and modifiedCount to confirm the scope of the change. A common mistake is forgetting the filter entirely when running updateMany — db. products. updateMany({}, { $set: { onSale: true } }) will update every document. Always preview with a find using the filter first. Takeaway: prefer update operators to preserve document shape and always verify counts after updates. Updating Documents with updateOne and updateMany means always use $set, $inc, $push and similar operators inside update documents to modify fields safely and avoid full-document replacement.. In practical terms, use update operators to change fields without overwriting documents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always use $set, $inc, $push and similar operators inside update documents to modify fields safely and avoid full-document replacement.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Update Documents
Core Concept

updateOne / updateMany with operators

Use operators inside the update document to modify fields. Without operators, the update replaces the whole document.

// update a single product

db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Laptop Pro" },
  { $set: { price: 1250.00 }, $inc: { stock: 5 } }
)

// update many products from a brand

db.products.updateMany(
  { brand: "ClickTech" },
  { $set: { available: false }, $push: { features: "Bluetooth 5.0" } }
)
Explanation
$set replaces or creates specific fields. $inc adjusts numeric values. $push appends to arrays. Combine them for multi-field updates.
Common mistake
Omitting operators will replace the entire document. Always include $set or other operators, unless a full replacement is intended.
Key Takeaway

Use update operators to modify only intended fields and check matchedCount/modifiedCount to confirm the effect.

screens.title: Deleting Documents Safely with deleteOne and deleteMany
screens.narratorSegment: Deletion must be handled deliberately because it is often irreversible. deleteOne removes a single document that matches the filter, while deleteMany removes all documents matching the filter. Before running a delete, preview the affected documents using the same filter with find. For example, run db. products. find({ available: false }). pretty() to inspect what would be removed, then db. products. deleteMany({ available: false }) if you confirm. A critical mistake is running deleteMany with an empty filter, which deletes all documents in the collection. Another risk is using an overly broad filter that unintentionally matches more documents than intended. After deletion, check the operation's deletedCount to confirm how many documents were removed and run a follow-up find to ensure the expected data is gone. Takeaway: always preview with find, confirm your filter, and read deletedCount — this habit prevents accidental data loss in development and production alike. Deleting Documents Safely with deleteOne and deleteMany means always preview with find and check deletedcount after running deleteone or deletemany to confirm the operation's effect.. In practical terms, remove documents with precise filters and verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: The _id Field and ObjectId Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Every MongoDB document has an _id field that uniquely identifies it within a collection. If you don't supply an _id when inserting, MongoDB creates one automatically, typically as an ObjectId. This ObjectId encodes a timestamp and other bits, providing a unique value generated by the database driver. Using the insertedId from insertOne or indexed _id values in a find query is the most reliable way to retrieve a newly created document. A common misconception is that _id is an integer counter; it is not. Another pitfall is attempting to match ObjectId as a string — when querying by _id, use the exact type returned, for example using the ObjectId wrapper in application drivers or the insertedId value from the shell result. Takeaway: rely on _id for direct lookup and use the returned insertedId or the correct type when constructing queries to avoid mismatches. The _id Field and ObjectId Behavior means _id uniquely identifies documents; use insertedid or the proper objectid type when querying by _id to ensure correct matches.. Core Concept

_id uniquely identifies documents

MongoDB provides an _id automatically if absent. ObjectId contains a timestamp and ensures global uniqueness for lookups.

Prefer direct lookups by _id using the actual returned insertedId or proper ObjectId typing to avoid errors.

screens.title: Single vs Multi-Document Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between single and multi-document commands depends on intent and risk. Use insertOne, updateOne, and deleteOne when you need a targeted change — for example, editing a user's profile or deleting a single record by _id. Use insertMany, updateMany, and deleteMany when you genuinely intend to affect multiple documents, such as applying a holiday price change across a product category. The trade-offs include control versus breadth: single-document commands are safer by design because they limit scope, while multi-document commands can be efficient but risk wide-impact mistakes if filters are too broad. A common mistake is accidentally using updateMany with an empty or loose filter, unintentionally changing all documents. Another important point is operation reporting: updateMany and deleteMany return counts showing exactly how many documents were matched or deleted — use these to audit the change. Takeaway: pick the narrowest command that accomplishes your goal, preview with find, then execute and verify results. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build fundamental fluency with the mongosh interactive shell. We begin by switching to or creating a database, then insert single and multiple documents, query with operators, update fields safely using update operators, and finally remove documents with care. These operations are the bread and butter of application data work: inserting records when users submit forms, querying to display results, updating to reflect state changes, and deleting when data is removed. A concrete example you will practice is managing a small products collection — inserting a Laptop Pro, querying by brand or price, incrementing stock, and deleting out-of-stock items. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls, such as accidentally replacing entire documents when you forget to use update operators, or removing everything by passing an empty filter to deleteMany. By the end you’ll understand each CRUD method syntax, when to use single‑document versus multi‑document variants, and how to craft filters with operators like $gt, $lt, and $in. Keep an eye out for the hands-on bookstore activity where you’ll try these commands yourself and confirm each change using find and findOne. Ready to begin and see how these commands map to real application needs?

These objectives focus your practice on the essential actions in mongosh and why each matters. First, you will perform CRUD operations in mongosh, which means using insertOne and insertMany to add records, find and findOne to query them, updateOne and updateMany to change them, and deleteOne and deleteMany to remove them. Practically, this means you can build features like product listing, search filters, inventory adjustments, and controlled removals. Second, you'll learn to craft query filters with operators such as $gt, $lt, $in and logical operators like $or and $and so you can select exactly the documents you need. Third, you will use update operators such as $set, $inc, and $push to change fields without overwriting entire documents, avoiding a common data-loss mistake. Finally, you'll practice safe deletion patterns and verification steps so you never accidentally remove the wrong records. Each objective pairs a command with a real example and a short verification step so you can measure your competence.

This second objectives slide zooms into patterns and verification steps you need to be reliable. You will practice using the use command to select or implicitly create a database, so you understand where your collections live and how MongoDB creates them on first insert. You will learn to inspect operation results: insertOne returns an insertedId and acknowledged status; update operations return matched and modified counts; delete commands return deleted counts. Recognizing these outputs helps verify success without blindly trusting state. You will also practice distinguishing single‑document commands from multi‑document variants and when each is appropriate — for user edits use updateOne, for sweeping changes across many records use updateMany combined with careful filters. Lastly, you will rehearse safety checks such as running a find with the same filter before executing deleteMany. This reduces catastrophic mistakes and builds a habit of verification.

Switching to the correct database is the first step in any shell workflow. The mongosh command use myStore doesn't throw an error if the database doesn't yet exist; instead MongoDB will implicitly create the database and any collection inside it when you first insert data. This behavior matters because operations like insertOne and insertMany will determine where your documents are stored based on the current database. A concrete example: running use myStore and then db. products. insertOne({ name: "Laptop Pro", price: 1200 }) creates myStore and a products collection if they didn't exist before. A common misconception is believing use creates a persistent database immediately; it only reserves the name until there is real data inserted. Another pitfall is running commands in the wrong database because you forgot to call use — your insert may quietly go to a different database. To avoid this, adopt a quick verification step: after switching, run show collections or a simple find to confirm the target collection exists or is empty. Takeaway: always set and verify your database context before mutating data to keep operations deterministic and safe.

Inserting documents is how you create persistent records in MongoDB. Use insertOne when you need to add a single document and insertMany when adding a batch. Each insert returns a result object: insertOne gives you acknowledged and insertedId; insertMany returns acknowledged and an array of insertedIds. For example, insertOne with a product document will return insertedId which you can then use to query that document. insertMany is useful during bulk imports — here you receive a map of inserted ids so you can cross-reference them or log creation. A common mistake is assuming insertMany is atomic across documents; while it inserts many documents in one call, partial failures can occur depending on options like ordered:false. Another pitfall is relying solely on the shell output without verifying with a find. After inserting, run db. collection. find({ _id: insertedId }) or db. collection. find(). pretty() to confirm. Takeaway: choose insertOne for individual writes, insertMany for batches, and always verify inserted IDs to ensure no silent failures. Inserting Documents with insertOne and insertMany means always read the returned insertedid(s) and perform a verification query to confirm the inserted documents exist as expected.. In practical terms, add single or multiple documents and verify insertion results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Queries are how you read data out of MongoDB. The primary methods are find, which returns a cursor that can match many documents, and findOne, which returns the first matching document. When you call find without a filter it returns all documents; when you pass a filter document you specify exact field conditions. For example, db. products. find({ brand: "TechCorp" }). pretty() returns all TechCorp items, while db. products. findOne({ name: "Laptop Pro" }) returns a single product. It’s important to understand how query operators extend filters: using price: { $gt: 100 } selects documents where price is greater than 100. A common misconception is expecting find to return an array immediately; instead it returns a cursor you iterate or print. In mongosh, chaining. pretty() formats output for readability. Takeaway: choose find when you expect multiple matches and findOne when a single result suffices, and always use filters and operators to limit data scanned for performance and correctness. Querying with find() and findOne() means use find for multi-document results and findone for a single match; always apply filters and operators to narrow results.. In practical terms, retrieve documents and use filters to narrow results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Query operators are the tools that let you find exactly the documents you need. Numeric comparison operators like $gt and $lt let you select values above or below thresholds — for example, price: { $gt: 100 } finds items costing more than one hundred. The $in operator matches any value in a provided array, useful for brands or enum fields. Logical operators $or and $and let you combine clauses: $or selects documents matching any clause, while $and requires all clauses to be true. A practical example: to find items from KeyMaster or ClickTech you can use { $or: [ { brand: "KeyMaster" }, { brand: "ClickTech" } ] }. Another example: find products with features containing "RGB Backlight" by querying the array directly with features: "RGB Backlight". A common misunderstanding is thinking $in is a subset test; it matches any listed value, not require all. Also avoid overly broad filters that unintentionally match many documents. Takeaway: use operators to narrow results precisely and test queries with find() before using them in updates or deletes. Query Operators — Filters and Logic means combine comparison and logical operators to build exact filters; test filters before using them in write operations.. Updating documents in MongoDB requires care: an update without an operator will replace the entire document. Choosing between single and multi-document commands depends on intent and risk. Use insertOne, updateOne, and deleteOne when you need a targeted change — for example, editing a user's profile or deleting a single record by _id. Use insertMany, updateMany, and deleteMany when you genuinely intend to affect multiple documents, such as applying a holiday price change across a product category. The trade-offs include control versus breadth: single-document commands are safer by design because they limit scope, while multi-document commands can be efficient but risk wide-impact mistakes if filters are too broad. A common mistake is accidentally using updateMany with an empty or loose filter, unintentionally changing all documents. Another important point is operation reporting: updateMany and deleteMany return counts showing exactly how many documents were matched or deleted — use these to audit the change. Takeaway: pick the narrowest command that accomplishes your goal, preview with find, then execute and verify results.
